summary: Fire behaves differently in microgravity, but the evidence needed to study spacecraft fire safety is scattered across experiments, tables and reports. flamingo is an AI-assisted research dashboard that connects questions to traceable NASA evidence. Researchers can discover relevant investigations, inspect source excerpts and compare original conditions while preserving ranges, approximations and provenance. Our collection includes 25 selected NASA PSI investigations, 2,009 nonblank source rows and 364 publication references. Hybrid keyword and semantic search helps users find related evidence even when wording differs. A separate Learn area introduces students to the science through clearly labeled educational illustrations. Our contribution is a practical question-to-evidence workflow that supports further analysis while making coverage and uncertainty visible.
details:
flamingo — From research questions to traceable NASA evidence

Flame Learning & Analysis in Microgravity: INsights for Gravity-Off missions

THE PROBLEM

NASA’s combustion research provides valuable evidence for studying fire prevention, detection and suppression in space. However, that evidence is distributed across investigation descriptions, experimental tables, calibration workbooks, documents and large media archives.

Researchers must identify relevant studies, recover their experimental context and assess whether their results support a particular comparison. Differences in fuels, oxygen levels, pressure, geometry, ventilation and measurement methods make this process challenging.

OUR SOLUTION AND USERS

flamingo is a publicly accessible, AI-assisted research dashboard for combustion researchers, aerospace engineers, educators and students.

It connects a research question to relevant investigations and inspectable evidence. Users can review experimental context, compare reported conditions, follow source locations, and export supported comparisons for further analysis.

Our response to Flame in Freefall supports three core actions:

  • Summarize: explore study objectives, experimental context, and available evidence.
  • Rank: retrieve relevant passages through keyword and semantic search.
  • Support interpretation: inspect original conditions and source documentation before concluding.

flamingo’s research interface: a question-led entry point to 25 NASA investigations and 2,009 available source rows. Background footage credited to NASA Johnson.

OUR RESEARCH WORKFLOW

  1. Ask a research question. Begin with a topic such as airflow calibration, smoke detection, or droplet extinction.
  2. Discover relevant evidence. Hybrid search retrieves original excerpts and source-backed investigation suggestions.
  3. Inspect the context. Open an investigation to review its objectives, available records, coverage, and references.
  4. Compare reported conditions. Compare up to four investigations or select two to six original source rows, retaining ranges, approximations, and missing fields.
  5. Trace and export. Follow source identifiers and available locators, then export supported comparisons as CSV.

A CONCRETE EXAMPLE

A researcher asks: “Can one fan calibration be applied to every BASS-II test?”

flamingo helps locate calibration-workbook evidence and related documentation. Source notes describe configurations organized by restrictors and calibrations that may be incomplete for a given day. This information helps the researcher identify what must be checked before applying a calibration to a particular record.

Another example is the comparison of Saffire-I oxygen entries: “21.5 - 21.7” and “~ 21.5” remain visibly different. The system preserves the interval and approximation instead of replacing them with one exact value.

These examples connect discovery with contextual interpretation. Displaying records together does not automatically establish scientific comparability.

Source-preserving comparison: Saffire-I records displayed side by side, retaining original oxygen ranges, approximation markers and source locators.

NASA DATA AND COVERAGE

Our collection includes 25 selected NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations: 24 classified as Combustion Science and one included for cabin-aerosol context.

The inspectable core contains:

  • 2,009 nonblank source rows across 22 tables.
  • 6,177 evidence items, represented by 3,152 retrieval fragments.
  • 364 publication references, whose full texts are not all acquired.
  • A separate curated reading room containing two complete PDFs.

The catalog summarizes approximately 12.3 TB of declared remote assets. These files have not all been downloaded or analyzed. We index a focused evidence core and preserve links to NASA’s larger collection.

HOW THE AI WORKS

A pretrained BAAI BGE-small-en-v1.5 model represents questions and source fragments as numerical vectors. Cloudflare Vectorize retrieves semantically related candidates, while keyword retrieval supports exact identifiers and technical terms. Reciprocal rank fusion combines the result lists.

The backend resolves candidate identities against the versioned corpus and returns original excerpts with source locations. The Research guide connects users to known investigations and their evidence.

The public AI capability is evidence discovery. Public OpenAI/Groq text generation is disabled. A separately labeled recorded evaluation demonstrates bounded GPT source selection; replaying it makes no new model request.

OUR CONTRIBUTION

Our contribution is the integration of semantic discovery, structured scientific evidence, provenance, comparison, and educational access into one research workflow.

We implemented structured acquisition and controlled extraction, source-preserving adapters, a versioned retrieval corpus, hybrid search, and a public interface. We use pretrained models; we did not train a new combustion predictor.

LEARNING AND ACCESSIBILITY

A dedicated Learn area offers three schematic 3D habitats, an illustrative flame lab and a science mission. These activities introduce students to relevant concepts and connect exploration with the research collection.

They are educational illustrations, not validated combustion simulations, emergency procedures, or certified habitat designs.

VALIDATION AND REPRODUCIBILITY

Our engineering checks include 60 backend tests and 23 frontend route checks. Source hashes and snapshot checks support artifact integrity.

In a seven-question development probe, an expected source appeared among the first three results in 6/7 keyword cases and 7/7 hybrid cases. This is a small development diagnostic, not a general accuracy benchmark.

The public repository includes source code, snapshots, tests, architecture documentation, and tools to reconstruct a local SQLite evidence store and reproduce the shipped corpus without model calls.

INTENDED IMPACT AND NEXT STEPS

Flamingo aims to make NASA combustion evidence easier to discover, inspect and reuse for spacecraft fire-safety research.

Next steps include broader evaluation with researchers, additional priority sources, and source-reviewed interpretation notes. User time savings and real-world safety improvements have not yet been measured. Applying orbital evidence to lunar or Martian environments requires independent assessment of the physical conditions.

AI ASSISTANCE AND CREDITS

ChatGPT/Codex and Claude supported development, debugging, data-organization tooling, and documentation drafts. Runtime semantic discovery uses a pretrained embedding model. NASA measurements, documents, and footage retain their source identities and credits.

Educational illustrations created with AI-assisted code are labeled in the application. Some presentation images are AI-generated. Our team produced the demonstration video. Further AI-use information is available on the website and in the repository.
